narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition emerged in 15th-century Italy, where dance masters first codified steps and etiquette.
Knowledge was preserved in manuscripts and later in printed manuals, with the earliest detailed instructions appearing between 1450 and 1460.
These practices spread across Europe, with significant contributions from French and English sources by the late 16th century.
on_screen: Map: Italy · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dance was a social activity and a marker of education and status.
It was used for display and entertainment at court, but also functioned as a communal activity that could be joined by anyone present at social events.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Renaissance Dance Bands 1551 1599, Tylman Susato Thomas Morley ( Centurys Recording David Munrow) (https://archive.org/details/renaissance-dance-bands-1551-1599-tylman-susato-thomas-morley-centurys-recording-david-munrow)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are performed either as couples or in groups (circles/lines).
Technique varies by style: 'basse danse' involves feet kept low to the floor, while 'haute danse' features energetic leaps and lifts.
Partners may hold each other, with some dances like the volta requiring intimate holds and lifts.
Watch for Volta lift.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Italian masters Domenico da Piacenza, Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro, and Antonio Cornazzano.
In France, Thoinot Arbeau is noted for his 1588 treatise 'Orchésographie'.
The tradition is documented across Italy, France, and England, with specific regional preferences for dances like the branle in France or the Chiaranzana in Italy.
Renaissance dance evolved from medieval dance traditions and laid the groundwork for later courtly and social dance forms in Europe.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Renaissance dance (Italy). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress: the sources do not describe the costume yet
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction
